transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-09-15
Time: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Cruz (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Ben Howard (Redwood Product), Sam Lee (CTO, NovaChat), Maria Gonzalez (ML Eng), Rajiv Patel (SRE), Tina Wu (Product)

Summary:
Quick migration walkthrough for NovaChat moving from a mix of OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood API. Focus on parity mapping (chat completions, function calls, embeddings), streaming behavior, cost/latency tradeoffs, security (VPC/KMS/SOC2), and next steps to run a pilot benchmark.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on the account, with Priya our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Sam: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to see how this could simplify our stack.
[00:13] Priya: Great. Quick agenda: we'll do a short product walkthrough - API parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood, console demo (routing/Optimize recommendations), and then discuss pilot/bench plan. We can dive deeper on security too.
[00:25] Maria: Head's up - our main concerns: latency under 200ms p50 for short chat turns, cost per 1M tokens, and keeping function-calling parity for our agent orchestration.
[00:35] Alex: Perfect, that's exactly what we'll focus on.

--- API parity mapping ---
[02:10] Priya: So first, mapping. For chat endpoints you're used to POST to chat.completions or /v1/chat for OpenAI, Redwood exposes a similar chat endpoint: POST /v1/chat - payload shape is intentionally similar: messages array, model, temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop. We also support function calling; syntax is close to OpenAI's function schema but with small differences - we return function_call metadata in the response and you can configure auto vs manual.
[03:05] Maria: Are there differences in the schema for nested objects in the function params? Sometimes our tools rely on strict typing.
[03:12] Priya: Good question. Redwood accepts the same JSON schema definitions for functions. We do add an optional field for schema_version in case you want to pin a compatibility shim when you run dedicated/private. But in typical hosted usage you shouldn't need to change your function definitions.
[03:35] Rajiv: Streaming - does streaming behave the same as OpenAI? We rely heavily on partial tokens for UI latency.
[03:42] Priya: We offer chunked streaming with the same SSE-like behavior. One small caveat: for some quantized model variants we batch token production aggressively; we expose the batch window config and you can tune for strict low-latency streaming or higher throughput. We'll demo the console setting under Optimize.

[06:10] Alex: Mapping for parameters: temperature, top_p, presence/ frequency penalties map 1:1. max_tokens is supported; we also surface token accounting differences in the Console (we show token counts per prompt and per response). For embeddings, the endpoint is /v1/embeddings - similar to OpenAI, but model IDs differ; Redwood provides a compatibility alias so you can call the same model name you use today and we'll route to the closest equivalent.
[07:05] Maria: Together has slightly different tokenizer behavior for some models - any gotchas?
[07:12] Priya: Tokenization can vary by model family; we provide a small tokenizer utility and mapping table in the migration doc so you can compare token counts. For billing and unit tests we recommend running your primary prompt set to see per-prompt token deltas.

--- Console / Optimize demo ---
[09:30] Ben: Jumping into the Console - here we have per-route dashboards. You can see token cost, latency histograms, error traces. Under Optimize we have suggested batching and quantization profiles based on observed workload - e.g., pick int8 or int4 variants if you accept small quality tradeoffs for big cost wins.
[11:02] Tina: Will those recommendations be actionable via API or only via Console?
[11:06] Ben: Both - we have recommended config JSON you can apply via our infra API or through the Console UI. For Dedicated customers we can also bake those defaults into the node provisioning template.

[13:40] Priya: Routing policies - important for you since NovaChat has EU users. You can route by region, by cost tier, or by model capability. We support fallbacks so if your preferred model is at capacity we can route to a cheaper/compatible variant automatically.
[14:04] Sam: How do we ensure the fallback doesn't regress quality?
[14:10] Priya: Great question - we provide eval hooks tied to prompt sets: you can flag a canary rollout and Redwood will only route traffic after passing a quality threshold on your test prompts, otherwise it will auto-fallback to the original model.

--- Security / Deployment modes ---
[17:20] Alex: Quick overview of deployment options: hosted (fastest), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools, SLA), Private (VPC/on-prem). For regulated data you likely want Private or Dedicated with VPC peering. We support KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HSM) and produce audit logs for every request.
[18:02] Rajiv: Audit logs format? We need request/response ids but not full response payloads in logs.
[18:10] Alex: We can redact responses - logs include request id, model, token counts, route, latency, and a hash/trace id you can use to fetch the full transcript if you have proper access.
[18:25] Maria: SOC 2? ISO?
[18:28] Alex: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II in scope and we have ISO 27001 in progress; we'll attach the security pack link. (link: https://redwood.example.com/security-pack)

--- Technical deep dive snippets ---
[20:00] Priya: For performance: our runtime does continuous batching and KV-cache sharing for chat workloads. That means if you have heavy context reuse (e.g., system prompt + recent turns) we can cache KV states and reduce compute per token. For yours, where many users have similar system prompts, it'll help a lot.
[20:45] Rajiv: Any special config for session affinity?
[20:50] Priya: Yes - we recommend sticky routing for low latency interactive sessions so KV cache stays warm on the same GPU. We can configure that per-route.

[22:30] Alex: Cost discussion - you mentioned 1M token cost baseline. For an apples-to-apples mapping we usually run your prompts and then provide a cost projection across hosted vs dedicated. Dedicated typically reduces unit cost by 30-60% depending on utilization.
[23:20] Sam: How long are typical commit windows for Dedicated?
[23:24] Alex: Monthly or annual commits; we'll show a few tiers. We can also do hybrids: dedicated for peak + hosted fallback for burst.

--- Migration concerns & parity examples ---
[25:00] Priya: Live example: we converted one of your sample prompts. (reads) Current OpenAI call: POST /v1/chat/completions with messages, model: gpt-4o, temperature: 0.2, functions: [...]. Redwood call is essentially the same: POST /v1/chat, model: redwood-g-4o (aliasing available), messages same, function schema same. Key differences: redwood uses an explicit request_id header for tracing, and we recommend sending a client_session_id for sticky routing.
[27:10] Maria: What about rate limits? We had per-second burst limits on OpenAI - we don't want unexpected 429s in prod.
[27:18] Priya: We expose per-key soft rate limits and per-route quotas. For Dedicated customers we can configure much higher burst and throughput. We also have a token-based backpressure system so long-running calls don't block short ones.

[30:00] Alex: Edge cases - embeddings: dimensionality mapping and model differences. We support same vector sizes for the major families and provide an embeddings-compat layer. For tooling we have sample code to swap the endpoint: keep your call structure, change base URL and model name, and run the provided tokenization diff script. Link: https://redwood.example.com/migration-guide#embeddings

[32:15] Tina: Do we need to change our chunking/embedding pipeline? We currently use Together embeddings for semantic search.
[32:22] Priya: Maybe minimal changes. We'll provide a notebook with exact steps: ingest, re-embed, compare recall/precision. In many customers we've seen parity within noise, but you should run the prompt set.

--- Bench plan & Pilot ---
[34:40] Priya: Pilot proposal: 1) Redwood runs a dev benchmark using 3 canonical prompts you provide, measuring latency p50/p95, quality (auto eval scripts), token counts. 2) We compare hosted vs dedicated with suggested quantization. 3) We'll produce a cost/latency report and recommended config. Can we target a 2-week pilot window?
[35:10] Sam: Yes, 2 weeks works as long as we can do an early read after a few days.
[35:18] Alex: We'll need an API key and a small sample dataset - action items noted.

--- Customer objections / clarifications ---
[38:00] Maria: Concern: deterministic function outputs - Together had slightly different random seeds behavior for deterministic tasks.
[38:10] Priya: You can set seed/temperature near 0 and we have a deterministic mode on some model builds. We'll mark deterministic variant in the mapping doc.
[38:30] Rajiv: Support model rollouts - we need canary and instant rollback.
[38:36] Ben: Console supports canary rollouts with traffic percentages and automatic rollback if your quality metrics dip.

--- Wrap-up and recap ---
[45:00] Alex: To recap: we'll send the migration parity doc, sample mapping table, pricing/tiers, and the benchmark plan. Redwood will run the first dev benchmark after you send 3 sample prompts and a dev key. Security pack attached.
[45:25] Sam: Sounds good. If we like the numbers we want to discuss Dedicated pricing and an initial commit.
[45:33] Alex: Great - Priya, any final notes?
[45:36] Priya: I'll follow up with a proposed benchmark timeline and invite for a results review 1 week after the run.
[45:45] Tina: One quick ask - can you include an example of switching from Together's client SDK to Redwood's client in Node? Small snippet is fine.
[45:53] Alex: Yep, we'll include migration snippets for OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood in our doc bundle.

[47:00] Maria: Thanks everyone.
[47:03] Alex: Thanks - we'll follow up.
